A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multimodal causal representation learning work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical simulations, constructed MNIST experiments, and human-phenotype data analysis in Section 6, Figure 5, Table 2, and Figure 6.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical work and reports redesigned MNIST results and additional simulation results in Appendix E, Figure 8, and Table 4.

M1.justification: The core reconstruction, independence, and sparsity estimator remains, but v2 adds contrastive preprocessing/loss to recover shared latent variables and treat shared blocks as separate modalities. Appendix E also introduces validation-loss-based selection of latent dimensionality, extending the procedure beyond v1's fixed-dimensional formulation and speculative masking suggestion.

E1.justification: Although both use colored and fashion MNIST, Section 6.2 replaces class-label, color, and rotation relationships with horizontal-position, transparency, vertical-position, and grayscale relationships. Appendix E additionally evaluates cyclic structures within/across modalities and shared latent variables. These change the represented causal scenarios; human-phenotype coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Figure 5 and Table 2 retain BetaVAE, CausalVAE, and MCL, with MCL still excluded from the four-modality numerical case. The new Appendix E experiments introduce no additional comparator. Gresele et al. appears in the revised related-work table, not as a newly evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E adds controlled evaluations using 30-dimensional observations with two, five, or six modalities, candidate latent dimensions from 1 to 10 selected using validation loss, and sample-size sweeps from 10,000 to 40,000. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Newly disclosed optimizer and training settings in Appendix F do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: The original sparsity ablation in Figure 5(c) remains. Appendix E adds scalability tests, latent-dimension selection analysis, sample-size sensitivity, and tests involving cyclic structures and shared variables, reported in Figure 8 and Table 4. These investigate several previously untested applicability and robustness questions.

E5.justification: v1 already displays uncertainty through error bars and plus/minus entries but does not explain their statistical basis. Appendix F.2 in v2 newly states that random seeds were used and results were averaged with variance reported. Seed values and run counts remain unspecified; an increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the MNIST results: the proposed method's R2/MCC means change from 0.89/0.87 to 0.90/0.85, and CausalVAE overtakes MCL in MCC. These concern redesigned data, not same-setting performance gains. Table 4 and Figure 8 add substantial results, including cyclic-setting MCC values of 0.89 and 0.92. Figures 5 and 6 retain their original results.

T1.justification: Condition 4.3 replaces the overlap/rank-based cancellation bound with a strict sparsity-increase condition under non-permutation block transformations. Theorem 4.4's sparsity requirement and Appendix C.2 proof are correspondingly revised. New Appendices C.3-C.4 introduce shared-block definitions, generalized identifiability conditions, and Theorems C.7 and C.9 with proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims of nonparametric, sparsity-based component-wise identifiability and a practical estimator supported by simulations and human-phenotype analysis. The biomedical terminology and shortened conclusion do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a Markov-equivalence qualification and physiological interpretations linking FRight3 to intraocular pressure, grip strength, and cataract. Appendix E expands applicability discussions to cycles, shared variables, and latent-dimension selection. Conversely, Section 7 removes v1's explicit dense/spurious-connection limitations and suggested alternative assumptions.

D1.justification: New Appendix F and Table 5 disclose modality-specific MLP, ResNet18, convolutional-decoder and LSTM architectures, adjacency masking, flow components, Adam/StepLR optimization, GPU use, a 10,000-epoch limit, early-stopping patience of 20, and dataset-specific loss weights. These are newly documented details, not established architecture changes. Appendix D.1 also drops v1's explicit Gaussian sampling and 50%-75% sparsity-range specifications.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds causal-discovery framing and citations, while Table 1 adds Gresele et al. and replaces nonlinear mixing with latent dependency as a comparison axis. References supporting identifiability, flows, and biomedical interpretation are updated, and the specific cancellation-bound novelty comparison is removed. The central positioning against parametric assumptions and subspace-only identification remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and theoretical explanations undergo extensive rewriting. Related-work paragraphs are reordered, terminology is standardized, and the conclusion is shortened. The title changes from biological to biomedical observations, acknowledgments are added, and the appendix organization expands with the existing pseudocode moved from Appendix E to G.

P2.justification: Figure 3 replaces a sparse-matrix sketch with a causal-graph illustration, and Figure 7 redraws the MNIST panel with its revised causal relationships. Figure 8 and Tables 4-5 add sensitivity plots, extended results, and architecture documentation. Table 1 changes its comparison structure. Several retained figures and tables are also relocated without changing their results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially reduces important documentation and validation gaps: Appendix F/Table 5 supplies previously absent architecture and training information, while Appendix E tests latent-dimension selection, sample sensitivity, scalability, and additional causal scenarios. Explicit shared-variable conditions and proofs support the methodological extension. These gains outweigh the removal of useful theoretical caveats, although run counts and some implementation details remain unspecified. The redesigned MNIST scores themselves do not establish improved performance.
